narrativeProgression.description: The interviewee begins to analyze the 'breaking India forces.'
He transitions to discussing Pakistan's interest in weakening India.
He further explores forces that aim to divide India, including NGOs and those motivated by 'so-called human rights.'
The discussion shifts to Islam's historical role in the partition of India and its present-day implications.
The focus turns to the impact of liberalism and social reforms in India.
The interviewee addresses the promotion of certain rape cases as a tool to negatively portray India.
He delves into the lack of response and responsibility from the BJP government in addressing the 'breaking India' campaign.
He concludes by emphasizing the importance of raising awareness and promoting consciousness among the people.

scenes.thematicElements: The interviewee discusses various forces that work to break India apart, including religious, political, and external influences. He analyzes the positive impact of liberalization and social reforms in India. He criticizes the use of specific incidents to negatively portray India and the role of the BJP government while emphasizing the need for awareness.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: You see there are breaking India forces at work that do want to break up India.
They are not as such America or China. They just take reality as it comes.
And so if there is an India here in this part of the world, well that's what they deal with.
They don't support separatism in Spain in favor of Catalonia.
But if Catalonia manages to become independent, then they will just notice and adapt their diplomacy accordingly.
So in the case of India too, it's not so much a matter of other countries.
Well, yeah Pakistan, that's a different matter. Pakistan has an interest in making India weak.
Not necessarily dividing it, keeping it bleeding by hundreds of cuts.
As one of the Pakistani leaders said, that is already something of course.
And so all this terrorism against India, that's part of the strategy of keeping India weak.
Other forces are probably even more ambitious.
You see you have all these NGOs, all these non-governmental organizations, often Christian or motivated by so-called human rights.
And so they are very much working against India and trying to divide India or trying to make pieces of it independent.
Dravidas, Tal and the South and getting Kashmir out of India and some of the Northeastern states and so on.
But then as for Islam, well, it's not against India.
With partitioning India in 1947, it has of course succeeded in acquiring a part of the subcontinent.
At the time when Islam was only 24% of the population here.
So that's already good.
But you see they've also learned that this has divided the Muslims.
And so maybe that was not the best strategy looking backwards.
I mean all the best parts of India have gone to the Indian Republic.
And so they have the left overs.
And then India is administered relatively well.
I mean I don't want to make publicity for all the Babu's in the Indian administration or so.
But nevertheless, you see there is freedom, there is lots of private initiative that is going well.
Socialism has, you know, ensured a long stance still economically of India.
India was for a long time proverbial synonym with poverty.
Like the time of Mother Teresa.
You know, but that's no longer the case.
You see the liberalization has sufficiently released the energies of the Indian people.
So that there's plenty of entrepreneurship.
Plenty of things are happening. There's plenty of progress.
So that's good. But you see socialism has also ensured a measure of necessary reform.
And I'm not at all holding a brief for socialism in general.
Nevertheless, the fact that there was land reform.
That there was social reform, that there was access to land property, to education and so on.
For formerly untouchable costs.
You see this desire for social reform by which India distinguishes itself from Pakistan, which is still a feudal medieval state.
You know, that is beneficial.
I am rather in favor of that.
So India has a pretty progressive country in the good sense of the word.
Nevertheless, you see all these NGOs are pushing human rights precisely in those points where they can use them to put Hindus in the dock.
And that is the reason why India is so important.
Because India is a very important country to like for instance, the nearby case.
Before that, India was known as a poor country.
As a country with a very unpleasant bureaucracy and so on.
But nevertheless, extremely interesting country.
People love to come here.
Nowadays, I hear many lady friends say, yeah, but India, that's so dangerous for women.
You know, these cases of rape have been enormously promoted, have been given enormous front page coverage.
And so by now, they are part of the image of India.
And wrongly so, I mean, what rape cases have taken place in Pakistan?
Do you know, I mean, in Belgium, at such a distance, I never read anything about rape cases in Pakistan, or in Australia, or in China, or wherever.
You see, when India something happens and they bring it to the front page in the West, that means there is an agenda behind it.
Not necessarily of that Western newspaper.
Usually they don't know what is going on in India.
But you see in India, they've promoted it.
They've positive in such a way as to be an attack on Hinduism, on native culture.
And then it becomes a little bit interesting.
And then they start taking it over. And then it takes on a life of its own.
And then ultimately, it starts making the image of India.
So that's where we are now. You can see what Rajiv Malhotra calls the breaking India forces.
You know, active enough to black and India.
And so that is very much going on.
It's a different kind of blackening than 50 years ago, but it's there.
And so now the second part of your question, well, you have to counter all that.
And so I do not have a fantastically clever strategy for that.
And the first thing to do is to just oppose it, to resist it, and to answer it.
You see, whenever you see that kind of attack on Hinduism, on Hindu culture, on native culture in general, in newspapers, on TV programs, you react against it.
And that's the first thing everybody can do.
Then to some extent, of course, this is also something that only a government can do.
Namely, to, for example, nominate the right people in positions of responsibility, nominate vice-chancellors in universities, for instance,
nominate people in charge of news programs and so on, to counter the systematic breaking India campaign.
But there you see, I find the BJP government doing very little, understanding very little of what it's all about,
probably because of an inferiority complex, like the borough many concepts from the secularists.
Like you have this idea that Hindus are naturally overbearing majority that has to be kept in check, like a dangerous dog has to be kept in his cage.
And so, yeah, I mean, many people who are nominally Hindu or Hindu-twa, nevertheless, have interiorized those assumptions.
And so, that's why they are slow in encountering it.
So, inferiority complex is one thing, another is simply that they don't care.
Now, in the BJP, many people have joined it, who have no ideological interest in it at all, who simply want to be on the winning side.
And they get positions of responsibility, which from the old guard, I find irresponsible, that they give positions of responsibility to just interlopers.
So, and then those people are ideologically uninterested, then you have people who well have other interests.
You see, like many people want economic reform. And so, they don't have the right to security concerns, to cultural concerns and so on.
So, that too is part of the problem. So, in all those cases, what you need is to activate them, to make them more conscious, more aware of the importance of this.
For that, again, there is no magic formula. Here I am reminded of what Ramasvaroop said, namely, that to light a candle, what you can use is another already burning candle.
And so, from candle to candle, you pass on the light. And so, in that sense, you see, you just have to work everywhere where you are, where you encounter fellow human beings.
And it is spread consciousness. That is very important, because if people don't know what they are doing, they are not going to do much, or not going to achieve much.

youtube_description:
The Belgian orientalist and indologist Koenraad Elst was with us, to tell his story. The writer of several books like, “The Saffron Swastika” and “Decolonizing Hindu Mind” talked about his childhood, his upbringing and his love for India, in this interview. He also answered several questions about religion, Hinduism and its impact on the society. To be a part of this beautiful journey, Check out our new Episode on Gap Sap: https://youtu.be/nyrHHb0wshk
